verses.51:21: And my inmost being was stirred to seek her out; therefore I have acquired a good possession.
verses.51:22: The Lord gave me a tongue as my reward, and with it I will praise Him.
verses.51:23: Draw near to me, you who are uninstructed, and lodge in the house of instruction.
verses.51:24: And because you say that you are lacking in these things, and your souls thirst exceedingly,
verses.51:25: I opened my mouth and spoke, "Acquire her for yourselves without silver;
verses.51:26: put your neck under the yoke, and let your soul receive instruction; she is near to be found.
verses.51:27: See with your own eyes that I labored but a little, and found for myself much rest.
verses.51:28: Partake of instruction with a great sum of silver, and acquire much gold through her.
verses.51:29: May your soul rejoice in His mercy, and may you not be ashamed in His praise.
verses.51:30: Do your work before the time, and He will give your reward in His time."

notes.1:6: The Greek critical text follows the shorter ancient Greek tradition (GI) and therefore omits verses 5 and 7 (as well as verse 21), which appear in expanded Greek manuscripts. The noun translated "skillful designs" (panourgeumata) carries a positive sense here of wisdom's subtle craftsmanship.
notes.1:13: The Greek text reads "he shall find favor"; several later manuscripts read "he shall be blessed."
notes.1:15: The vivid Greek phrase "made an everlasting foundation her nest" (enosseusen) reflects the Greek translator's rendering of the underlying Hebrew, picturing wisdom's lasting dwelling among humanity.
notes.1:19: The opening clause "He saw her and numbered her" echoes verse 9 and establishes the Lord as the subject of the actions that follow; it is omitted in some manuscripts.
notes.1:29: Literally "in the mouths of men," an idiom referring to putting on a false front before the speech and opinion of others.
notes.2:9: Literally "for gladness of eternity and of mercy," where both genitives depend on "gladness" in the Greek.
notes.2:14: The verb "visits" (episkeptetai) carries the biblical sense of God's decisive inspection and judgment.
notes.2:18: The Greek uses the future indicative ("We will fall") with a cohortative force, echoing David's words in 2 Samuel 24:14.
notes.3:5: The middle clause ("and he who glorifies his mother is like one who stores up treasure") repeats verse 4 verbatim in the Greek critical text.
notes.3:10: The Greek text reads "in dishonor" (pros atimian) rather than the variant "a father's dishonor" (patros atimia) found in some manuscripts.
notes.3:14: Literally "will be built up additionally for you," signifying that mercy shown to a father stands as a lasting credit offsetting sins.
notes.3:26: The Greek critical text places the clause on loving danger first with "will fall into it" (rather than "will perish") and doubles the clause concerning a stubborn heart at the last.
notes.4:13: The subject of "enters" is unexpressed in Greek and may refer either to the one who holds fast to Wisdom or to Wisdom herself.
notes.4:16: The Greek text shifts abruptly from the second person ("If you trust, you will inherit her") to the third person ("his generations"), continuing in the third person through verse 19.
notes.4:23: Some later Greek witnesses add a second line warning not to hide wisdom in its beauty, which is absent from the Greek critical text translated here.
notes.4:30: The rare Greek participle phantasiokopon literally denotes being given to wild fancies or delusions, referring in context to erratic, suspicious, or frantic behavior toward one's household.
notes.5:14: The Greek reads the passive verb ἐνεδρευθῇς ("be ensnared" or "ambushed"), whereas some manuscripts read the active ἐνέδρευε ("lay snares").
notes.5:15: In this Septuagint versification, verse 5:15 encompasses the text numbered 5:15–6:2 in some editions. The closing clause faithfully renders ὡς ταῦρος ("like a bull"), a well-known Septuagint reading where the Hebrew may have had a different image.
notes.6:5: Literally "a sweet throat" (λάρυγξ γλυκὺς), a Semitic idiom for pleasant, gracious speech.
notes.6:20: The Greek text reads ταχεῖα ("swift"), preserved by major uncial manuscripts, whereas other witnesses read τραχεῖα ("harsh" or "rough").
notes.6:22: Wisdom's hiddenness "according to her name" reflects a Hebrew wordplay between musar ("discipline" or "instruction") and mustar ("hidden") that lies behind the Greek rendering.
notes.6:29: The Greek text reads οἱ κλάδοι αὐτῆς ("her branches"), whereas other manuscripts read οἱ κλοιοὶ αὐτῆς ("her collars"), echoing verse 6:24.
notes.7:17: In this Greek text, the warning "Remember that wrath will not delay" stands in the middle of verse 17 rather than at the end of verse 16 as in some editions.
notes.7:18: "Money" translates Greek adiaphoron (literally "an indifferent thing," used here for material gain); "Souphir" preserves the Septuagint form of Ophir.
notes.7:31: This Greek text reads "from the beginning" (ap' arches) before listing the priestly portions prescribed in the Law, including the "gift of the shoulders" (cf. Deut 18:3).
notes.7:36: The Greek text reads "in all your words" (logois), whereas some textual witnesses and the Hebrew tradition read "works" or "ways."
notes.8:2: "Outweigh you in the balance" renders a weighing-scale metaphor (literally "counterbalance your weight"), referring to a wealthy person's power to sway judgment.
notes.8:5: "Under penalty" (Greek en epitimois) means liable to punishment or judgment for one's own sins.
notes.8:11: "Rise up in the presence of" reflects the Greek idiom for reacting with provocation or confrontation, warning that an insolent person lies in wait to trap one's words.
notes.8:19: The second clause literally reads "let him not bring back a favor to you," warning against placing oneself under obligation to an untrustworthy confidant.
notes.9:5: The Greek phrase literally refers to her penalties or fines, alluding to the legal penalties incurred under the Law for seducing or wronging a virgin (cf. Exodus 22:16-17; Deuteronomy 22:28-29).
notes.9:13: The Greek verb literally means to suspect or apprehend, warning against placing oneself in constant apprehension of death before a ruler who holds power over life.
notes.10:7: The Greek clause is syntactically compressed and is rendered here with pride as subject, though the neuter plural for unjust deeds may also be construed as the subject ("unjust deeds will be an offense against both").
notes.10:9: The critical Greek text preserves an abrupt first-person aorist verb ("I have cast away"), referring to God casting away a mortal's inward parts even while alive.
notes.10:10: The Greek reads "the physician mocks" (or scoffs at) a lingering illness, underscoring the suddenness with which even a king's life ends.
notes.10:17: The Greek verb means "He withered" or "dried up," continuing the imagery of uprooting nations from verse 15.
notes.10:27: This Greek text reads directly "works in all things than he who strolls about, or...," lacking the expansion "and abounds in all things" found in some manuscripts.
notes.11:6: The Greek critical text reads "companions" (hetairon), whereas some manuscripts read "others" (heteron).
notes.11:17: Verses 15 and 16 are absent from the main Greek critical text (appearing only in later expanded witnesses), so the verse numbering moves directly from verse 14 to verse 17.
notes.11:20: Greek diatheke ("covenant") here reflects the Hebrew sense of one's allotted obligation or appointed task.
notes.11:30: A "decoy partridge in a basket" refers to a caged bird used by hunters to lure other birds into a trap.
notes.12:8: The Greek critical text reads ekdikethesetai ("will be vindicated" or "avenged"), whereas the Hebrew text and some Greek witnesses read "will not be known."
notes.12:11: This difficult Greek clause literally says "it has not completely corroded," picturing the vigilance needed to see through an enemy's humble pretense as one inspects a wiped bronze mirror.
notes.12:15: Greek ou me karterese ("will by no means stand firm") can also carry the sense "will not hold back" from turning against you when you stumble.
notes.13:8: The Greek text reads "in your gladness" (en euphrosyne sou), whereas the Hebrew text reads "in your folly."
notes.13:12: "He who does not guard words" refers to a powerful ruler who mercilessly fails to keep spoken words in confidence and uses them to punish his guest.
notes.13:24: The critical Greek text reads "in the mouths of a godly man" (en stomasin eusebous), whereas some Greek manuscripts and the Hebrew text read "of the ungodly."
notes.14:12: Greek diatheke ("covenant," also in 14:17) here denotes an appointed decree or fixed term set by Hades.
notes.14:16: Greek apateson (literally "beguile") is used here in the sense of indulging or treating oneself, reflecting the Hebrew sense of pampering oneself.
notes.14:20: The critical Greek text reads teleutesei ("shall die"), whereas the Hebrew text and some Greek witnesses read "meditates" (meletesei).
notes.15:11: The critical Greek text reads second-person ou poieseis ("you shall not do"), whereas other Greek witnesses and the Hebrew text read third-person "He will not do."
notes.15:14: Greek diabouliou ("counsel") reflects the Hebrew term for inward inclination or moral deliberation, emphasizing human free choice.
notes.15:15: The compact Greek phrase pistin poiesai eudokias ("to practice faithfulness is a matter of good will") can denote either acting faithfully by one's own willing choice or practicing the faithfulness that pleases God.
notes.16:9: "Nation of destruction" translates Greek ethnos apoleias (reflecting the nations devoted to destruction), and "swept away" renders exermenous, which can also mean "lifted up" in arrogance.
notes.16:14: Verses 16:15–16 are absent from the primary Greek critical text and are omitted accordingly.
notes.16:27: Greek archas can mean either "dominions" (referring to the appointed realms of the heavenly luminaries) or "beginnings."
notes.17:3: The Greek text reads the plural kath' heautous ("befitting themselves" or "according to themselves"), whereas some manuscripts read the singular kath' heauton ("like Himself").
notes.17:8: The Greek text reads ton ophthalmon autou ("His eye"); some later manuscripts read "His fear." Verses 17:5, 17:9, 17:16, 17:18, and 17:21 are absent from the primary Greek critical text.
notes.17:13: The Greek critical text literally reads phones auton ("their voice"), whereas other witnesses read phones autou ("His voice").
notes.17:31: The Greek syntax places poneros ("an evil man") in the nominative and sarka kai haima ("flesh and blood") in the accusative; some versions invert the grammar to "flesh and blood devises evil."
notes.18:12: "Forgiveness" renders Greek exilasmos (also in 18:20), which in the Septuagint denotes both atonement/propitiation and divine pardon.
notes.18:18: "Wastes away the eyes" renders Greek ektekei ophthalmous, a vivid idiom for causing bitter grief or weeping over a grudgingly given gift.
notes.18:23: Greek euxasthai can mean either "to make a vow" or "to pray"; following the mention of vows in 18:22, it refers primarily to making a vow.
notes.18:30: The section heading "Self-control of the soul" (Greek Enkrateia psyches) stands in the Greek manuscript tradition at the beginning of this verse.
notes.19:5: The critical Greek text reads kardia ("in heart"); some Greek manuscripts read kakia ("in wickedness"), yielding "he who rejoices in wickedness shall be condemned."
notes.19:13: Greek elenxon (repeated in 19:14, 19:15, and 19:17) encompasses confronting, questioning, and reproving, culminating in the allusion to Leviticus 19:17 in 19:17.
notes.19:23: Greek poneria literally means "wickedness" (echoing 19:22), whereas the underlying Hebrew tradition contrasts malicious "cleverness" with simple folly.
notes.19:27: "Feigning deafness" renders the rare Greek compound heterokophon, literally pretending to be deaf on one side while covertly watching for an advantage.
notes.20:14: The idiom "his eyes are many in place of one" indicates that the fool gives grudgingly while expecting many favors in return for a single gift.
notes.20:22: "Shame" here denotes misplaced bashfulness or fear of losing face; "because of a foolish person" translates the Greek idiom "from a foolish face," meaning out of undue deference to a fool.
notes.20:27: "Words of proverbs" is an ancient internal section heading preserved directly in the Greek text.
notes.21:5: The Greek pronoun "His" implicitly refers to God despite no prior explicit antecedent; in the second clause, it may alternatively be read as "his judgment," meaning the poor man's vindication.
notes.21:8: The Greek literally reads "for winter," an image of futile or self-defeating labor (some scholars suspect an underlying Hebrew wordplay on a burial mound or tomb).
notes.21:25: The Greek text reads "shall be weighed down" (echoing v. 24), contrasting the burdensome talk of meddlesome strangers with the measured words of the prudent weighed in a balance.
notes.21:27: Greek "ton satanan" transliterates the Hebrew title meaning "the adversary" (Satan), which may refer either to the demonic adversary or to an opponent whom the ungodly man blames for his own guilt.
notes.22:9: Verses 22:7–8 are absent from the primary Greek text tradition (G-I) and appear only in later expanded witnesses.
notes.22:13: Greek entinagmos ("spattering" or "shaking off") vividly recalls the image of shaking filth off the hand in 22:2.
notes.22:17: Greek kosmos psammotos refers to a sand-plaster or stucco adornment applied to a polished wall, illustrating durable inner steadiness.
notes.23:2: The Greek reads "their sins" (auton), referring to the thoughts and heart (or the unguarded lips of 22:27), with the singular verb pare ("pass over") agreeing with "discipline."
notes.23:7: "Discipline of the mouth" is an ancient Greek section heading preserved within the text of 23:7, and the closing phrase "by his own lips" continues directly into 23:8.
notes.23:8: Greek kataleiphthesetai (literally "will be left behind") reflects a common orthographic variant for katalephthesetai ("will be caught" or "overtaken"), paralleling "caught" in 23:7.
notes.23:14: The Greek text has third-person singular synedreuei ("one sits in council"), where some manuscripts read second-person "you sit," and resumes the warning at the end with me katarase ("lest you curse").
notes.23:17: The lines numbered 23:16 in some editions are joined to the beginning of 23:17 in this Greek versification.
notes.24:6: Greek ektesamen means "I gained a possession" (or "acquired"); some manuscripts read hegesamen ("I held sway" or "ruled").
notes.24:14: Greek en aigialois literally means "on the shores" (or "along the banks"), whereas other textual traditions read "in En-gedi."
notes.24:27: Greek hos phos literally means "like light," likely reflecting a Hebrew wordplay or confusion between ye'or ("the Nile") and 'or ("light") alongside the other great rivers in vv. 25-27.
notes.24:34: Greek auten ("it" or "her") refers back grammatically to teaching (didaskalian, v. 33) and more broadly to Wisdom throughout the chapter.
notes.25:1: Greek horaisthan ("I was adorned") and anesten horaia ("I stood forth beautiful") use the feminine form, representing the speaker's soul (cf. he psyche mou in v. 2).
notes.25:9: Greek phronesin means "prudence" or "good sense"; the surviving Hebrew text reads "a true friend."
notes.25:15: Greek kephale ("head") literally renders Hebrew rosh, a word that means both "head" and "venom/poison."
notes.25:17: Greek hos sakkon means "like sackcloth"; the surviving Hebrew text reads "like a bear."
notes.26:5: The Greek phrase "before a fourth countenance I have made supplication" is unusual and likely reflects a Hebrew expression for being terrified before a fourth thing, which is introduced in verse 6.
notes.26:10: The Greek text reads the adverb "unswervingly" modifying the command to strengthen the watch; some manuscripts read the dative adjective "headstrong" modifying "daughter."
notes.26:18: The Greek text reads "breast" (literally plural, "breasts/bosom"), which many scholars regard as an early copyist variant for "heels" matching the pillar-and-base imagery.
notes.26:28: Verses 19–27 are absent from the primary Greek manuscript tradition (GI) and appear only in expanded secondary witnesses (GII).
notes.27:1: The Greek text reads "a trifle" (literally "an indifferent thing"); some manuscripts read "profit" or "gain."
notes.27:18: The Greek text reads "his enemy"; some manuscripts and versions read "his dead" (i.e., someone lost to death).
notes.27:23: The Greek text reads "your mouth" (speaking sweetly to please you); some manuscripts read "his mouth."
notes.28:1: The Greek uses an emphatic participial construction (literally 'firmly fixing, He will fix') to stress that the Lord keeps a strict account of the vengeful person's sins.
notes.28:14: 'A third tongue' translates a Semitic idiom for a slanderous or meddling third party who comes between two others.
notes.28:21: Literally 'and Hades is more profitable than it,' using the genitive of comparison to emphasize that even the grave is preferable to the ruin brought by a slanderous tongue.
notes.29:6: The Greek text reads 'not for nothing' (ou dorean), meaning the lender has acquired an enemy at his own expense; some other manuscripts omit the negative to read 'without cause.'
notes.29:8: The Greek text lacks the negative particle present in some manuscripts ('do not keep him waiting for alms'), reading positively that one shall draw the humble person toward mercy.
notes.29:17: The second half of this verse ('it has uprooted mighty men...') is numbered separately as verse 18 in some editions, so the verse numbering here proceeds directly from 29:17 to 29:19.
notes.29:23: The Greek text preserves the shorter reading here, without the additional clause ('and you shall not hear the reproach of your sojourning') found in some later manuscripts.
notes.30:1: The opening heading "Concerning children" translates an ancient Greek superscription preserved in the manuscript tradition of Sirach.
notes.30:7: The Greek text here reads "concerning the lives of sons" (as in Codex Vaticanus); other Greek witnesses divide and read the letters as "he who pampers a son."
notes.30:13: The Greek text here reads "lest he stumble in your disgrace"; other Greek manuscripts read "lest you stumble at his disgrace."
notes.30:25: Literally "a bright and good heart will care for its foods at meals," signifying that a cheerful disposition takes healthy nourishment from its food.
notes.31:2: The verbs rendered "banishes" and "dispels" literally mean "demands back" and "wakes soberly from," reflecting unusual Greek renderings of the underlying proverb.
notes.31:5: The Greek text here reads "will himself be filled"; other Greek manuscripts read "will go astray in it."
notes.31:13: "From every face" literally renders a Greek phrase reflecting a Hebrew idiom meaning "because of everything" or "in the presence of all."
notes.31:21: "Rise up and step away" translates the Greek phrase literally meaning "rise up going in the midst"; other Greek witnesses read "vomit outside," matching the Hebrew text.
notes.32:17: Greek synkrima here means a comparison or precedent, referring to a self-serving justification or ruling found to excuse one's conduct.
notes.32:18: The closing clause is syntactically obscure in Greek (literally, 'even after doing with him without counsel'), conveying that the arrogant man remains fearless even after acting on his own without advice.
notes.32:23: The Greek text reads 'trust' (pisteue) rather than the Hebrew reading 'guard' your soul, emphasizing conscientious integrity in one's actions.
notes.33:3: This Greek text reads dikaion ('an inquiry of the righteous'), whereas other Greek witnesses and editions read delon ('an inquiry of the Urim').
notes.33:17: In this Greek text, numbering moves directly from verse fifteen to verse seventeen without the opening clause ('And I, the last, kept watch') found in some manuscripts.
notes.33:31: 'With blood' is an idiom expressing that a servant was acquired at heavy personal cost, comparable to one's own lifeblood or livelihood.
notes.33:32: This Greek text reads 'as yourself' (rather than 'as a brother' in some witnesses) and literally says 'as your soul, there is need of him.'
notes.34:9: The Greek text reads "well-instructed" (pepaideumenos), whereas some critics conjecture "traveled" (peplanemenos) to parallel verse ten.
notes.34:18: The Greek reads "mocked" (memokemene) and "mockeries" (mokemata), standing alongside the variant "blemished" (memomemene) attested in some manuscripts.
notes.35:17: In this Greek versification, verses seventeen through twenty-two span material sometimes subdivided across additional verse numbers; in verse twenty-one, "righteously" translates the adverbial reading dikaios rather than the dative variant "for the righteous."
notes.35:24: The Greek literally reads "in the time of his affliction," with the singular pronoun referring collectively back to "His people" in verse twenty-two.
notes.36:7: The Greek reads "oath" (horkismou), whereas the Hebrew text reads "appointed time."
notes.36:10: The clause "I also, the last, kept watch" is preserved in this Greek text as a textual seam remnant from the ancient manuscript transposition involving Sirach 33:16.
notes.36:13: The Greek text reads "Your people" (ton laon sou), whereas the Hebrew and certain other witnesses read "Your temple."
notes.36:23: Literally "her husband is not according to the sons of men," an idiom meaning that he is uniquely favored beyond ordinary men.
notes.37:3: Greek ἐνθύμημα ("imagination" or "evil impulse") denotes a deceitful inclination, and ἐνεκυλίσθης literally means "were rolled in," picturing deceit engulfing the earth.
notes.37:11: Greek μισθίου ἀφεστίου literally designates a hired laborer living away from the hearth or household ("an outside hireling"), contrasted with the resident household servant that follows.
notes.37:17: Greek ἴχνος ἀλλοιώσεως καρδίᾳ literally reads "a trace of alteration is in the heart," introducing the four contrasting outcomes in verse 18 that spring forth and are governed by the tongue.
notes.37:30: Greek χολέρας refers to severe bilious or intestinal illness resulting from overindulgence.
notes.38:8: The subject of συντελέσῃ ("will bring to an end") may be understood either as God, whose healing works never cease, or as the apothecary, who can never exhaust God's works.
notes.38:11: Greek ὡς μὴ ὑπάρχων literally means "as one who is no more," urging a generous offering as though facing death rather than clinging to worldly possessions.
notes.38:19: The Greek phrase ἐν ἀπαγωγῇ παραβαίνει καὶ λύπη is difficult; ἀπαγωγή ("carrying away" or "affliction") and παραβαίνει ("goes alongside" or "passes by") depict grief accompanying calamity, while κατὰ καρδίας expresses what weighs against the heart.
notes.38:28: Greek καινιεῖ literally means "will renew," describing the hammer's sound ringing perpetually anew in the smith's ear, though some textual witnesses and commentators understand a verb meaning "to deafen."
notes.38:30: The Greek text reads τὸ χάρισμα ("the gift"), a reading found in major early manuscripts, whereas another textual tradition reads τὸ χρίσμα ("the glaze").
notes.39:11: The Greek omits the comparative before "than a thousand," and the verb rendered "it suffices for him" reflects an unusual Greek rendering of an expression meaning to have enough or be satisfied.
notes.39:13: The Greek text reads "by a stream of the field," whereas some other witnesses read "by a stream of water."
notes.39:28: Greek pneumata can mean either "spirits" or "winds"; the masculine plural pronouns and personified fury favor "spirits" as agents of divine judgment.
notes.39:35: The Greek text has the first-person plural "we have sung praise" alongside the imperative "bless," whereas many manuscripts read the imperative "sing praise" in the first clause as well.
notes.40:1: The Greek text reads "until the day of burial into the mother of all," where some manuscripts read "the day of return to the mother of all."
notes.40:9: The Greek text here lists four calamities; some manuscripts add a second clause naming afflictions, famine, ruin, and scourge.
notes.40:14: The first clause is terse and leaves its subject unspecified in Greek, contrasting the joy of one who opens his hands with the complete ruin of transgressors.
notes.40:18: The Greek text reads "a self-sufficient laborer" without a conjunction, though the following "above both" preserves the paired pattern of the proverb series in this section.
notes.40:25: The Greek text here reads "a wife is esteemed," whereas other Greek manuscripts and the Hebrew text of Ben Sira read "counsel is esteemed."
notes.41:4: The Greek word elegmos ('reckoning' or 'reproof') conveys that in Hades no one disputes or calls to account the length of a mortal life.
notes.41:9: The Greek text reads gennethete ('be born'), rather than the Hebrew reading 'increase' or 'multiply,' portraying the entire existence of the ungodly from birth to death as allotted to a curse.
notes.41:20: Leaning an elbow upon the bread reflects a breach of table etiquette, while skorakismos ('scornful dealing') denotes contemptuous or insolent behavior in financial exchanges.
notes.42:2: The Greek literally reads 'to justify the ungodly,' either continuing the warning against partiality in verse 1 or referring to rendering impartial justice even when an ungodly person is in the right.
notes.42:5: The Greek adiaphorou literally means 'impartial' or 'indifferent' (a textual variant alongside diaphoros, 'profit' or 'margin'), pointing to fair dealing in commerce.
notes.42:12: The Greek text literally reads 'do not gaze upon any person because of beauty,' differing from the Hebrew tradition that warns against exposing a daughter's beauty.
notes.42:18: The Greek text preserves the first-person verb dienoethen ('I have pondered'), whereas other manuscripts read third-person dienoethe ('He considered') referring to the Lord.
notes.42:21: The Greek reads kai heos estin ('and while He exists'), a textual variant for hos estin ('as He is'), affirming God's eternal, unchanging self-sufficiency.
notes.43:8: The Greek text reads parabolon ("of parables/comparisons"), where other Greek manuscripts read parembolon ("of armies/encampments").
notes.43:13: The Greek text reads katepausen ("caused to rest/stilled"), whereas other manuscripts read katespeusen ("hastened").
notes.43:17: The Greek text reads oneidisen ("reproached"), where other manuscripts read odinesen ("caused to travail").
notes.43:23: The Greek text reads ephuteusen auten Iesous ("Jesus planted it"), a notable scribal variant in major Greek uncials for ephuteusen en aute nesous ("He planted islands in it").
notes.43:26: The Greek text reads euodia ("sweet fragrance"), a manuscript spelling variant for euodia ("prosperous journey/success").
notes.44:3: The Greek text uses the future verb bouleusontai ("they shall give counsel"), whereas other witnesses read the participle bouleuontes ("giving counsel").
notes.44:11: The prepositional phrase "in the covenants" (en tais diathekais) stands at the end of verse 11 in the Greek text and completes its clause in verse 12.
notes.44:17: The Greek text repeats dia touto ("therefore the flood came"), whereas other Greek manuscripts read hote ("when the flood came").
notes.45:3: The Greek reads κατέπαυσεν ("caused to cease"), referring to Moses ending the plagues in Egypt by his word, whereas some manuscripts read κατέσπευσεν ("hastened").
notes.45:10: The Greek phrase δήλοις ἀληθείας ("manifestations of truth") is the Septuagint rendering corresponding to the Urim and Thummim on the high priest's breastpiece (cf. Exodus 28:30).
notes.45:15: "Filled his hands" renders the biblical Greek idiom ἐπλήρωσεν τὰς χεῖρας, denoting priestly consecration and ordination (cf. Exodus 28:41; Leviticus 8:33).
notes.45:16: The Greek abruptly shifts to second person (τοῦ λαοῦ σου, "your people"), addressing Aaron directly as in 45:22, whereas some manuscripts harmonize to third person.
notes.45:17: Major Greek witnesses read φωνῆσαι ("to proclaim to" or "to summon"), whereas other witnesses read φωτίσαι ("to enlighten").
notes.45:25: The Greek reads simply "a son of the tribe of Judah" without naming Jesse, though some later witnesses supply "son of Jesse."
notes.46:1: The phrase "according to his name, great for the salvation of His chosen ones" alludes to the Hebrew meaning of the name Joshua ("the Lord saves").
notes.46:3: Major Greek witnesses read τοὺς πολεμίους Κύριος αὐτὸς ἐπήγαγεν ("the Lord Himself brought the enemies forward"), whereas other witnesses read τοὺς πολέμους Κυρίου αὐτὸς ἐπήγαγεν ("he himself waged the wars of the Lord").
notes.46:13: Major Greek witnesses omit the name "Samuel" here and read singular βασιλέα ("a king") rather than βασιλείαν ("a kingdom"), though the passage clearly refers to the prophet Samuel.
notes.46:18: "Tyrians" follows the Septuagint Greek Τυρίων, which renders Hebrew tsar (meaning either "Tyre" or "adversary") as the people of Tyre.
notes.47:2: "Peace offering" renders Greek σωτηρίου, the standard Septuagint term for the fellowship or peace offering (cf. Leviticus 3:1–5).
notes.47:6: Major Greek witnesses read singular verbs ("He glorified... and praised"), whereas other witnesses read plural ("they glorified... and praised"), referring to the people honoring David's ten thousands (cf. 1 Samuel 18:7).
notes.47:20: Major Greek witnesses read the first-person verb κατενύγην ("I was grieved"), expressing the author's own lament over Solomon's folly, while other witnesses read the infinitive κατανυγῆναι ("to be grieved").
notes.48:11: The Greek text reads "adorned in love" (kekosmemenoi), whereas some commentators conjecture "fallen asleep in love" (kekoimemenoi) from the Hebrew. "Shall surely live" renders the Hebraic cognate construction "shall live with life."
notes.48:17: The Greek text reads "Gog," an inner-Greek transmission variant for the spring Gihon, whose waters Hezekiah channeled into Jerusalem through rock (cf. 2 Chronicles 32:30).
notes.48:18: The Greek text has a nominative subject ("his hand") with an active verb, rendered passively here as "his hand was lifted up," where some manuscripts read the accusative ("he lifted up his hand").
notes.49:6: The Greek text uses a singular verb ("it burned," matching "a foreign nation" in verse 5) followed by a plural verb ("they made desolate"). "By the hand of Jeremiah" refers to the fulfillment of the prophetic word spoken through Jeremiah.
notes.49:9: The Greek text reads "the enemies" (ton echthron), where the Hebrew text of Ben Sira refers to Job, whose Hebrew consonants closely resemble the word for "enemy."
notes.49:10: The Greek text has singular verbs ("comforted ... redeemed"), rendered here with the Lord as subject, whereas some Greek manuscripts read plural verbs referring to the twelve prophets.
notes.49:12: The Greek text reads "a holy people" (laon hagion), whereas some manuscripts read "a holy temple" (naon hagion).
notes.49:13: The Greek text reads the verb nemousin ("they bestow") rather than the proper name Neemiou ("of Nehemiah") found in other manuscripts, though the description of rebuilding the fallen walls, gates, and bars clearly refers to Nehemiah.
notes.50:3: The Greek text reads elattothe ("was diminished"), generally regarded as an early scribal variant for elatomethe ("was quarried" or "hewn out"), referring to the digging of a temple cistern.
notes.50:18: The Greek text reads "the vast house" (en pleisto oiko), referring to the temple precincts, whereas some manuscripts read "the fullest sound" (en pleisto echo).
notes.50:20: The Greek text reads the dative Kyrio ("to the Lord"), whereas other manuscripts read the genitive Kyriou ("the blessing of the Lord").
notes.50:21: The Greek text has a singular verb ("he bowed down a second time") and epideixasthai ("to show forth"), referring to the high priest, whereas other manuscripts read a plural verb and epidexasthai ("to receive"), referring to the people.
notes.50:26: The Greek text reads "the mountain of Samaria," whereas the Hebrew text reads "Mount Seir," referring to the Edomites.
notes.51:6: The Greek text reads enesen ("gave praise"), an early manuscript reading (as in Codex Vaticanus), whereas other witnesses read engisen ("drew near").
notes.51:10: The title "the Lord, the Father of my lord" translates the exact Greek Kyrion patera kyriou mou, a distinctive Septuagint rendering; the final clause ("And my prayer was heard") is counted as verse 11 in some editions.
notes.51:19: The Greek text reads en poiesei limou ("in the practice of hunger/famine"), where other Greek manuscripts read nomou ("of the law").
notes.51:20: The Greek text preserves the plural met' auton ("with them") in this clause order, where other manuscripts read the singular met' autes ("with her").
notes.51:28: The Greek text reads en pollo arithmo argyriou ("with a great sum of silver"), creating a rhetorical contrast with "without silver" in verse 25 and differing from traditions that read "a small sum."

unplaced.text: Since many and great things have been given to us through the Law and the Prophets and the others who followed after them—for which Israel ought to be praised for instruction and wisdom, and since not only ought the readers themselves to become knowledgeable, but lovers of learning should also be able to be useful to those outside, both in speaking and in writing—my grandfather Jesus, after devoting himself extensively to the reading of the Law and the Prophets and the other ancestral books, and having acquired considerable proficiency in them, was himself also led to compose something pertaining to instruction and wisdom, so that lovers of learning, becoming committed to these writings as well, might make much greater progress in living according to the Law. You are urged, therefore, to read with goodwill and attention, and to show forbearance wherever we may seem to fall short in some of the expressions over which we have labored in translation; for things spoken in Hebrew do not have the same force in themselves when carried over into another language. And not only these, but the Law itself, and the prophecies, and the rest of the books have no small difference when spoken in their original tongue. For when I came into Egypt in the thirty-eighth year under King Euergetes and remained for a time, I found a copy of no small instruction; I therefore judged it most necessary myself to apply some diligence and labor to translating this book. Indeed, I have devoted much sleepless effort and skill over that span of time to bringing the book to completion and publishing it also for those living abroad who wish to love learning, preparing their character to live according to the Law.
unplaced.note: The Greek translator's prologue by the grandson of Jesus ben Sira, dated to the thirty-eighth year of Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II (132 BC), is the earliest witness to the threefold division of Israel's Scriptures ('the Law and the Prophets and the other ancestral books') and reflects on the inherent challenges of translating Hebrew into Greek.

unplaced.note: Parallels the opening clauses of 41:27 in the site numbering.
